title: Consequence of dishonesty on another's self-perception
description: This latent activates on sentences that articulate how deception or withholding truth deprives another person of a positive self-image or emotional benefit (e.g., the chance to feel good, proud, or virtuous). It responds to reasoning structured as 'by doing X, you deny them Y,' specifically where Y is an internal emotional/psychological reward tied to identity or self-regard. It would not activate on general statements about lying being wrong, factual descriptions of deception, or sentences about consequences that are purely external (financial, physical, relational) rather than about the other person's self-concept or emotional state.

title: Validating a partner's relationship stance
description: This latent fires on sentences that offer empathetic validation of someone's relationship-related feelings or decisions, typically framed as 'it's reasonable/understandable that [person] would feel/do X' in the context of romantic partnerships. It activates on supportive, non-judgmental commentary that legitimizes a partner's priorities (like wanting children) or their potential reactions (like reconsidering the relationship) as valid rather than unreasonable. It would not activate on neutral factual statements about relationships, advice-giving that lacks this validating/legitimizing framing, or emotional support unrelated to interpersonal or romantic dynamics.

title: Suggesting alternative practical options
description: This latent fires on phrases that propose concrete alternative solutions or resources to a practical problem, typically framed as suggestions ('you could...', 'explore...', 'look into...', 'maybe we could...') listing specific services, activities, or arrangements (e.g., carpooling, babysitters, food banks, shared housing, hobby groups). It activates most strongly on advice-giving text that offers a menu of tangible options or workarounds for logistical, financial, childcare, housing, or social-activity problems. It does NOT activate on general emotional validation, moral judgments about behavior, restating someone's feelings, or purely interpersonal/relational advice that lacks a concrete actionable alternative (e.g., statements about boundaries, entitlement, or empathy without a suggested resource or option).

title: Transitional lead-in to a numbered list of advice
description: This latent fires on short introductory phrases like 'Here are some thoughts to consider:', 'Here's my take:', or 'I'll try to offer some advice/perspective' that immediately precede a numbered list (often followed by '1.' or '1. **'). It captures the specific discourse function of signaling that a structured, itemized response (advice, suggestions, points, tips) is about to follow, typically in an advice-giving or Q&A context. It activates most strongly on the boilerplate lead-in sentence itself and the initial list marker, rather than on the substantive advice content that follows. It does NOT activate strongly on the actual advice sentences, empathetic statements, judgments (e.g. 'You're not the asshole'), or substantive list items that make up the body of the response, even though these co-occur in the same passages.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet marker that begins an item in an enumerated list (e.g., '3.', '9.', '4. **'), rather than on any semantic content. It activates most strongly on bare digit tokens followed by a period, often immediately preceding bolded headers or list content, and also fires more weakly on the surrounding list text as part of a structured 'tips/steps/strategies' response format. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking an enumerated structure, or on list items that use bullets/dashes instead of numerals, since the trigger is specifically the numeric list-index marker rather than the advice-giving content itself.

title: Formulaic self-care encouragement closings
description: This latent fires on short, imperative or affirmational closing statements in advice/support contexts that directly address 'you' with formulaic encouragement to take care of yourself, prioritize your well-being, or affirm your worth and strength (e.g., 'Take care of yourself and prioritize your own well-being,' 'You are strong and capable, and you deserve...'). It activates most strongly on the canonical, high-frequency phrasings of this genre—'take care of yourself,' 'prioritize your well-being,' 'you deserve,' 'you're strong/capable'—especially when used as a terminal, motivational sign-off rather than embedded mid-argument. It activates more weakly on related advice-column content that discusses self-care, boundaries, or emotional well-being analytically or as part of a longer explanatory sentence (e.g., 'Practice self-care: take care of your physical and emotional well-being' within a numbered list, or 'it's essential to recognize that your mental health is valid'). It would NOT activate on sentences that give concrete situational advice, ask questions, analyze a relationship dynamic, or discuss other people's feelings/actions without directly issuing this reassuring, second-person affirmational closing formula.

title: Framing a decision as significant/impactful
description: This latent fires on sentences that characterize an upcoming choice or action as important, weighty, or consequential, typically by explicitly naming what it will affect (e.g., 'relationship', 'future plans', 'career'). It activates on evaluative framing statements that precede or accompany advice-giving, signaling to the reader that the stakes are high before details are discussed. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, on sentences that merely describe a decision's content without commenting on its importance, or on advice that lists concrete pros/cons rather than asserting significance in the abstract.

title: Enumerated list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens that begin items in an enumerated list (e.g. '2.', '3. **', '4.'), regardless of the list's topic or content. It activates most strongly on bare or bolded numeric markers introducing list points, often in structured advice or breakdown responses (e.g. 'Here's why: 1.', 'Let's break it down: 2.'). It does NOT activate on the prose content of the list items themselves (the explanatory sentences that follow), nor on numbers used in other contexts like dates, quantities, or statistics -- the key trigger is the numeral functioning as a list-item delimiter/marker.

title: Attributing responsibility for concealment/deference in a relationship
description: This latent activates on sentences that summarize or reflect back to someone their role in hiding, denying, or deferring to another person's wishes within an interpersonal relationship. It fires on statements that assign agency ('she's the one who...', 'you've been...') for concealment or accommodating behavior, often in a therapeutic, advice-giving, or interpersonal-conflict framing. It would not activate on neutral factual statements about relationships, general descriptions of secrecy without attribution of who is responsible, or sentences lacking the second-person/reflective 'you've been respecting/doing X' structure that assigns blame or acknowledges deference.

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing of a situation
description: This latent fires on stock exclamatory openers of the form 'What a [adjective(s)] situation/topic/dilemma!' used to dramatically characterize a person's predicament as complex, sensitive, tricky, or emotionally fraught, typically as a rhetorical lead-in before offering advice or validation. It activates most strongly on these near-formulaic exclamations themselves, and more weakly on other similar empathetic framing devices (e.g. 'The eternal conundrum of...', 'The age-old debate...') that name and dramatize a situation's difficulty. It does not activate on plain descriptive or advisory statements that discuss a situation's complexity or sensitivity without the exclamatory 'What a ___!' or equivalent naming-the-dilemma construction, such as explanations of why something is understandable or validating statements like 'You are not the asshole' or 'That's understandable.'

title: Self-help advice list items
description: This latent fires on imperative, bullet-style self-improvement tips — short bolded headers ('Practice mindfulness**', 'Focus on strengths**') followed by brief instructional or motivational content about mindfulness, positive self-talk, building confidence, breaking goals into small steps, and finding joy in the present moment. It activates most strongly on formulaic advice-listicle phrasing (often with markdown bold and a colon) that prescribes a concrete coping or self-growth technique, and on generic reinforcing statements like 'this will help build confidence and momentum.' It does not activate on conversational, empathetic, or situational advice about interpersonal dynamics, relationship problems, or reasoning through a specific personal scenario, even when emotionally supportive language is present — the key trigger is the generic, list-item self-help technique format rather than advice content tailored to a particular narrative situation.

title: Numbered list items and empathetic follow-up questions
description: This latent fires on short, standalone conversational fragments: bare list-item numerals (e.g. '2.', '3.', '4.') and brief, formulaic supportive or clarifying questions such as 'Is everything okay?', 'What do you think?', and 'Can you tell me more about what happened/what's going on?'. These are typically terse, standalone utterances that either enumerate steps/points in advice-giving text or serve as empathetic conversational prompts inviting elaboration or emotional check-in, often at the start or end of a turn. It does not activate on longer descriptive or explanatory sentences that discuss feelings, relationships, or advice in full prose (e.g. sentences elaborating on someone's emotional state or reasoning), even though those sentences are topically similar; the latent specifically tracks the short, template-like question/numeral form rather than the underlying content.

title: Partial disagreement hedge phrase
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic hedging responses that partially negate or qualify a preceding claim or question, especially the stock phrases 'Not entirely' and 'Not necessarily' (often standing alone as a sentence). It activates most strongly on these exact minimal phrases, and more weakly on related contexts involving qualified judgments, advice-column style hedges, or moral verdicts (e.g., 'Not the a**hole', 'not unreasonable', 'not too late') where a claim is being softened or partially rejected rather than flatly affirmed or denied. It would not activate on full affirmations, flat denials ('No.'), or on substantive advice/explanatory sentences that don't center on this partial-negation hedge construction, even if they occur in similar advice-giving or moral-judgment contexts.

title: Advice to approach conversations calmly and empathetically
description: This latent fires on short imperative or list-item phrases that instruct someone to have a conversation calmly, respectfully, and with empathy or understanding, often as a numbered advice-list header (e.g., 'Approach the conversation with empathy and understanding,' 'Try to have a calm and rational conversation'). It also activates strongly on the bare list markers ('2.', '3.') that introduce such advice steps in structured relationship/conflict-resolution guidance. It is most active on the templated, formulaic phrasing itself (calm + respectful + empathy/understanding, often bolded as a step header) rather than on the surrounding substantive advice content. It does NOT activate strongly on sentences that give specific situational advice, describe someone's feelings or actions, or discuss the content of a conflict without using this stock 'approach calmly/respectfully/with empathy' framing, even though those sentences may be topically similar (about communication or relationships).
